when: Use this when you need to know who orders work or which event to use for a feedback conversation.
guidance: Keep product ordering with the product owner and enable the team to organize its work. Use a review to inspect the increment with stakeholders and a retrospective to improve how the team works.

distinction: The sprint review and sprint retrospective answer different questions about the product and how work happens.

title: Hybrid delivery and fixed commitments
aliases: ["hybrid project", "blended approach", "fixed dates and flexible scope"]
when: Use hybrid when part of the work needs fixed commitments and another part needs customer feedback.
guidance: Identify which milestones or scope are committed and what can evolve in the backlog. Agree how the team will report progress and who can approve changes that cross the boundary.
exam_reasoning: The course discusses a case with fixed contractual milestones and evolving requirements. Explain why both conditions matter before choosing hybrid.
approach_relevance: Use predictive controls on committed work and adaptive planning where requirements evolve; coordinate milestones across both.
distinction: Calling a project hybrid does not make a contractual date optional or put every backlog change through a board.

title: Predictive and adaptive delivery selection
when: Pick a way of working before committing stakeholders to the wrong kind of plan.
guidance: Use requirements stability and the need for feedback to choose how much planning to do up front. Revisit the choice when constraints or uncertainty change.
exam_reasoning: The instructor flags the comparison among predictive, adaptive and hybrid as study material. Read the scenario for constraints and uncertainty before picking an approach.
approach_relevance: Predictive uses more up-front planning; adaptive refines work through feedback. Hybrid can mix the two where project conditions differ.
distinction: Adaptive planning still happens. Choosing an approach does not remove the need to plan or manage change.

title: Project artifacts, PMIS and configuration control

guidance: Decide where plans and registers live, how people see the current approved version, and how to track changes. Use configuration controls for items that need version and change history.

distinction: A register tracks items such as risks or stakeholders. A management plan describes how to manage that work. Configuration control is a function, not simply a folder.

title: Baseline change control and backlog decisions
concepts: ["change request", "change control board", "baseline change", "impact assessment", "integrated change control"]
when: Use this when a request affects approved scope, dates, costs or contract commitments.
guidance: Record the request and evaluate impacts before seeking a decision from the appropriate authority. Keep a record of the decision and update approved plans if authorized. Route changes confined to evolving backlog work through the product owner's ordering process.
exam_reasoning: The instructor compares predictive and adaptive ways of handling a request. Identify whether a baseline or a backlog is affected before choosing the next action.
approach_relevance: Predictive work uses formal control for approved baselines. Adaptive work uses backlog refinement within agreed boundaries. Hybrid needs both routes and a clear boundary.
distinction: A request is an input to a decision, not approval to implement. Product backlog ordering is not a substitute for contractual approval.

distinction: Project acceptance marks a decision about delivery. Benefits may be measured after closure by the receiving organization.

title: Delivery cadence, pull and timeboxes
when: Use this when choosing between working in fixed-length periods and pulling new work as capacity opens.
guidance: Agree how often stakeholders need usable work or feedback. For flow, make active work visible and avoid starting more than the team can handle. For timeboxed work, use the iteration boundary to plan and inspect progress.

approach_relevance: Adaptive teams can use flow or timeboxes; hybrid teams should coordinate their cadence with any fixed milestones or release approvals.
distinction: A WIP limit constrains active work. It is not a forecast of how much work will be completed.

title: Risks, issues and impediments
when: Use this when something has already happened or a team is actively blocked.
guidance: Check whether the risk register already names a response or owner. Log the actual issue, assign a next action and review date, and escalate when the team cannot resolve it within its authority.

approach_relevance: Predictive teams may use an issue log. Adaptive teams often track impediments where the team sees them; hybrid uses agreed escalation routes across both.
distinction: An issue can create new risks. That does not make the issue itself uncertain again.

title: Risk analysis and threat or opportunity responses
concepts: ["risk register", "probability and impact matrix", "risk response", "threat", "opportunity", "risk owner", "trigger"]
when: Use this while an uncertain event could affect your objectives and there is time to prepare a response.
guidance: Record the uncertainty, rate probability and impact, then focus further analysis on decisions that justify it. Agree a response, owner and trigger. For threats consider mitigation or avoidance; for opportunities consider enhancing or exploiting them.

distinction: Risk mitigation is one response, not the name for all responses. A risk can be a threat or an opportunity.

title: Schedule baseline and variance

guidance: Approve a schedule benchmark, collect actual progress, and investigate differences before proposing action. Communicate the forecast separately from the approved baseline and use formal control for baseline changes.

approach_relevance: Use a baseline on predictive commitments and fixed hybrid milestones. Adaptive teams may track a release forecast separately from governed dates.
distinction: Updating the current schedule is not the same as replacing the approved baseline.

title: Schedule compression: fast tracking and crashing
when: Use this when the finish date needs to move earlier and removing scope is not an option under consideration.
guidance: Compare overlapping critical activities with adding resources to shorten them. Assess the rework risk or extra cost, check approval authority and recalculate the critical path after the change.
exam_reasoning: The instructor stresses that compressing work away from the critical path will not advance the overall finish unless the schedule logic changes.
approach_relevance: Apply to dependency-based scheduling in predictive or hybrid work. In adaptive work, reconsider what can fit in the release instead of assuming overlap improves delivery.
distinction: Fast tracking overlaps work; crashing adds resources, usually at a cost. Neither is the same as dropping scope.

title: Critical path and schedule dependencies
when: Use this when a date slips and you need to know which activities can move without delaying completion.
guidance: Build a network of dependencies with durations. Compare path lengths and calculate early and late dates to identify float. Recalculate as actual progress changes.
exam_reasoning: The instructor emphasizes identifying the longest dependent path and determining float from early and late dates.
approach_relevance: Use on predictive schedules or the fixed dependency network within a hybrid project. An adaptive team's flow metrics answer different questions.
distinction: A long activity is not automatically critical. Look at its path through the network.

approach_relevance: Adaptive work uses backlog ordering and refinement. Hybrid can use a backlog within the parts of scope that may evolve, subject to contractual or baseline boundaries.
distinction: A request entering the backlog does not mean it is committed for delivery. Backlog refinement is distinct from approving a baseline change.

guidance: Choose elicitation techniques for the stakeholders and question: interviews for individual detail, facilitated workshops for shared decisions, or observation to see the work. Record requirement sources and trace changes to downstream work.
exam_reasoning: The course reviews several elicitation techniques. Choose one based on the information and people in the scenario.
approach_relevance: Predictive teams can maintain an explicit traceability matrix. Adaptive teams refine backlog items with stakeholders. Hybrid teams can keep traceability for commitments while refining implementation details.
distinction: A list of requirements does not show their origin, changes or verification unless it records those links.

title: Conflict management and resolution
when: Use this when a disagreement begins to disrupt team decisions or relationships.
guidance: Find out what the parties disagree about and how severe it is. Help them acknowledge the problem and look for a resolution. Escalate when the severity or decision authority warrants it.
exam_reasoning: The instructor warns against ignoring conflict and uses Leas' levels as a study aid. Read the severity and context before selecting a response.
approach_relevance: Use team working agreements and direct conversation across approaches. A retrospective can surface patterns, but active conflict may need attention before the next retro.
distinction: Collaboration is a way to work toward a resolution; escalation changes who must act or decide.

title: Servant leadership and team empowerment
when: Use this when a team waits for permission on decisions it could own or when performance problems point to unmet needs.
guidance: Ask what is preventing the team from doing its work. Remove barriers, delegate within clear boundaries, and tailor your support to the team rather than taking over its decisions.
exam_reasoning: The course calls out autonomy and motivation. In a scenario, examine what support the team needs before adding control.
approach_relevance: Adaptive teams emphasize self-management. Predictive and hybrid teams can also delegate decisions while keeping organizational accountability clear.
distinction: Empowerment needs decision boundaries. It is different from leaving a team without support.
